title: Pachomius
hook: a former soldier organizes monks into communities with shared work and prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert mothers, and Amma Syncletica's warning that a crowd can live inside your head. Your word was amma, and your line was the desert is within. Where did you find the doorstep? Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Down the Nile goes a boatload of new recruits, kept under guard at night, more like prisoners than soldiers. One of them is a young Egyptian, just drafted into the army. At one town, strangers come down to the boat with food and drink and look after them. He asks who these people are. Christians, he's told. They're kind to everyone, for the sake of God. That night, the story of his life says, he made a promise: if he got free, he would serve God and serve people. His name is Pachomius.
screen: `DRAFTED, UNDER GUARD.` → `STRANGERS BRING FOOD.` → `A PROMISE THAT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the kindness keeps working. Released from the army, Pachomius is baptized, and he goes to learn the desert life from an old hermit named Palamon. Hard teaching: little food, long prayer, manual work. He learns it. Second, the new thing. Anthony's way, which we met three days ago, was mostly the way of the hermit, alone or nearly. Pachomius gathers monks into a community. At a deserted village called Tabennesi, the story goes, he begins to build. One wall around them all. One rule. One table. The monks work, weaving mats and baskets, farming, cooking, nursing the sick, and what they make is for everyone. They pray together at set times. An abbot leads, and the brothers obey him, not as a general but as a father. Third, why it matters. The hermit's life suits a few. A shared life can hold many: the strong and the weak, the gifted and the ordinary. Some readers see in his communities the picture in Acts, where the believers held all things in common. Shared work can wear off rough edges in a way solitude may not, because the brother who annoys you is at breakfast tomorrow. Catholic religious orders that live in community stand in that line. Fourth, look back at this week. Under persecution, they hid the books. With Constantine came freedom, and its dangers. Helena went to see. Anthony heard and went. Abba Moses said the cell teaches. Syncletica said the desert is within. And today Pachomius says something the desert needed to hear: you don't have to go alone. Together in the desert.
screen: `A HERMIT'S HARD SCHOOL.` · `ONE WALL, ONE RULE, ONE TABLE.` · `THE BROTHER AT BREAKFAST.` · `THIS WEEK, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `TOGETHER IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one task with others. Settle, and breathe. Think through the work of your day: dishes, a report, a ride to school, a load of laundry, a meal. Which one do you usually do alone, a little resentfully, or a little proudly? Choose one, and picture doing it beside someone else instead. Not handing it off. Doing it together, the way Pachomius's monks wove and cooked side by side. Picture who it is. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on the work the two of you will share. The bell holds the time.
Pachomius. A former soldier, won over by strangers' kindness, who gathered monks into communities of shared work and prayer. Today's word.
Your line: together in the desert. Today, ask someone to do one ordinary task with you, and do it side by side. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns who live in community share meals, work and the prayer of the hours under a rule and a superior, and the Church honors Saint Pachomius as a founder of that common life.

myth: Pachomius was a soldier before he was a monk
drafted as a young man; the kindness of Christians to the recruits turned him.
Pachomius's monks each lived alone and rarely met
they shared one wall, one rule, one table, work and prayer.
Pachomius taught himself the desert life
he first learned from an old hermit named Palamon.

fork.setup: you're a young recruit under guard on the Nile. strangers come with food and look after you. they're Christians. what do you do?
options: promise to serve God and people if you get free.
slip away with them that night.
fork.reveal: his life says he made that promise, and kept it: baptism, the hermit Palamon, and then a whole community.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing — the word Acts uses for the believers' common life.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks always lived alone in caves.
what it means: Pachomius gathered them into communities with one rule, shared work, shared meals and prayer at set times.
what a scholar hears: koinonia, the fellowship of Acts, lived behind a wall at Tabennesi under an abbot.

sources.ref: Life of Pachomius (Bohairic and First Greek Lives)

notes: Conscription, Christians feeding recruits on the Nile, his promise, release, baptism, training under Palamon and building at Tabennesi follow the Lives of Pachomius; paraphrased and hedged ('the story of his life says', 'the story goes'). Confirm details.
Description of the rule (one wall, shared work such as mat- and basket-weaving, set common prayer, abbot) is general; confirm.
'Pachomius's communities were living out the picture in Acts' is an interpretation; the Pachomian sources do appeal to Acts' common life. Confirm or soften.
Week-end day (715–721): teach looks back on the week's carries.
'Anthony's way, which we met three days ago' refers to day 718.
Editor: Acts link attributed to "some readers"; softened the absolute claim about shared work versus solitude.

Editor (second pass): hook no longer opens 'A young Egyptian...' three days after day 718's 'A young man in Egypt...'; now opens on the boat on the Nile. Practice's closing prayer changed from 'hold that person before God', used on days 712, 713, 715 and 724.
